  • Estudios sobre la historia monetaria y bancaria de Puerto Rico y del Caribe hispano de los siglos XIX y XX.
  • Archivos históricos sobre el Tratado de París (1898) y la transición del peso al dólar en las Antillas.
bodyHtml.en:
The history of banking in Puerto Rico is marked by its double colonial heritage: first Spanish and, from 1898, American. That transition was stamped on its banknotes and coins, which makes the island especially rich ground for notaphily.

Spanish Puerto Rico and its money

Until the late nineteenth century Puerto Rico was an overseas province of Spain. For generations a mixed metallic currency circulated on the island: Spanish colonial pieces, worn cobs, and foreign coins that arrived with trade. The shortage of a stable, trusted circulating medium was a recurring problem for the island economy and prepared the ground for a formal banking institution.

The Banco Español de Puerto Rico

The Banco Español de Puerto Rico, established in 1888 by royal provision, is usually considered the island’s first issuing institution. Besides the functions of a commercial bank —deposits, loans, and discount— it received the right to issue notes denominated in pesos, finally giving Puerto Rico its own organized paper money.

The Puerto Rican peso

In parallel, around 1895 a provincial coin specific to the island was struck, the Puerto Rican peso, with silver fractions. The Banco Español notes and these provincial coins formed a monetary system distinct from the peninsular one, designed for local commerce.

1898: from the peso to the dollar

The Spanish–American War and the Treaty of Paris of 1898 placed Puerto Rico under United States sovereignty. One of the most immediate and sensitive consequences was monetary: the Puerto Rican peso was withdrawn and replaced by the U.S. dollar, in an exchange at an unfavorable rate that meant a loss of value for many inhabitants of the island.

From Banco Español to Banco de Puerto Rico

The founding institution itself reflected the change of era: the Banco Español de Puerto Rico was renamed Banco de Puerto Rico in 1913, fully integrated into the dollar system. Its issues of the last decades of the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth rank today among the most prized pieces of Caribbean notaphily.

For the collector

The notes and coins of this period are tangible testimony of Puerto Rico’s passage from Spanish colony to U.S. territory. An emblematic example is the 1-peso exchange note of 1895, issued by the Ministerio de Ultramar in the last years of Spanish sovereignty. You can explore more examples in our Puerto Rico banknote catalog.

Sources

  • Standard Catalog of World Paper Money (Albert Pick), Puerto Rico section, for cataloguing Banco Español de Puerto Rico issues.
  • Studies of the monetary and banking history of Puerto Rico and the Spanish Caribbean in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
  • Historical archives on the Treaty of Paris (1898) and the peso-to-dollar transition in the Antilles.

bodyHtml.es:
Los billetes de un país son una galería de retratos que revela a quién honra su memoria colectiva. En Colombia, el papel moneda ha pasado de los héroes de la independencia a los grandes nombres de la cultura, contando de paso la historia del país.

Los héroes de la independencia

Durante buena parte del siglo XX, los rostros dominantes fueron los de la gesta independentista. Simón Bolívar, el Libertador, y Francisco de Paula Santander, “el Hombre de las Leyes”, aparecieron una y otra vez en las emisiones del Banco de la República —Bolívar, por ejemplo, en el clásico billete de 1.000 pesos—. A ellos se sumó Policarpa Salavarrieta, “La Pola”, heroína y mártir de la independencia, uno de los pocos rostros femeninos de aquella etapa.

Ciencia, letras y arte

Con el tiempo, el papel moneda amplió su panteón a figuras de la cultura y el pensamiento: escritores como Jorge Isaacs o José Asunción Silva, y científicos y humanistas que dieron nombre a distintas denominaciones.

La familia de billetes actual

La serie de billetes que el Banco de la República puso en circulación a partir de 2016 consolidó ese giro hacia la cultura. Entre sus protagonistas figuran la pintora Débora Arango (2.000), el poeta José Asunción Silva (5.000), la antropóloga Virginia Gutiérrez de Pineda (10.000), el estadista Alfonso López Michelsen (20.000), el Nobel de Literatura Gabriel García Márquez (50.000) y el expresidente Carlos Lleras Restrepo (100.000). Por primera vez, varias mujeres protagonizaron denominaciones completas.

Más que un retrato

Cada rostro viene acompañado de paisajes, motivos y símbolos que completan el relato: monumentos, fauna, geografía y escenas históricas. Leer un billete colombiano es, en el fondo, leer un fragmento de la identidad nacional.

Puede ver muchos de estos personajes y emisiones en nuestro catálogo de billetes de Colombia.

bodyHtml.en:
A country’s banknotes are a gallery of portraits that reveals whom its collective memory honors. In Colombia, paper money has moved from the heroes of independence to the great names of culture, telling the country’s story along the way.

The heroes of independence

For much of the twentieth century the dominant faces were those of the independence struggle. Simón Bolívar, the Liberator, and Francisco de Paula Santander, “the Man of the Laws”, appeared again and again on Banco de la República issues —Bolívar, for example, on the classic 1,000-peso note. To them was added Policarpa Salavarrieta, “La Pola”, heroine and martyr of independence, one of the few female faces of that stage.

Science, letters, and art

In time, paper money widened its pantheon to figures of culture and thought: writers such as Jorge Isaacs or José Asunción Silva, and scientists and humanists who gave their names to different denominations.

The current family of notes

The series Banco de la República put into circulation from 2016 consolidated that turn toward culture. Among its protagonists are the painter Débora Arango (2,000), the poet José Asunción Silva (5,000), the anthropologist Virginia Gutiérrez de Pineda (10,000), the statesman Alfonso López Michelsen (20,000), the Nobel laureate in Literature Gabriel García Márquez (50,000), and former president Carlos Lleras Restrepo (100,000). For the first time, several women starred on complete denominations.

More than a portrait

Each face comes with landscapes, motifs, and symbols that complete the story: monuments, fauna, geography, and historical scenes. To read a Colombian banknote is, in the end, to read a fragment of national identity.

You can see many of these figures and issues in our Colombia banknote catalog.
